column3: It directly joins an as-yet-unattained gain with God's encompassing power, closely paralleling the untraversed land.
Inheritance of the garden supports the gifted, rather than purchased, character of the outcome, though its setting is eschatological.
Permission to fight the wronged and God's power to aid them supplies the conflict premise for a divinely given outcome.
God's power to replace a people affirms sovereign control, but does not address territorial inheritance.
The immediately preceding verse recounts the defeat and captivity from which the land, homes, and wealth of 33:27 follow.
God's ownership of heaven, earth, and all within them, together with complete power, grounds the authority to bestow land and goods.
The accounting of good and bad intercession does not clarify inherited land or divinely granted spoils.
The doubters' denial of God's promise belongs to the same siege narrative whose resolution is expressed in 33:27.
God's making the righteous inherit a land for dwelling closely matches land as a bestowed inheritance, despite the garden setting.
The loss of homes and wealth by emigrants provides a meaningful contrast to their later divinely ordered provision.
The plea for a misguided father does not illuminate the focus verse.
Night worship's firmness of speech has no material link to territorial inheritance or divine bestowal.
It expressly says the earth belongs to God and that He makes whom He wills inherit it.
The reward for obedience in the Prophet's household does not clarify the transfer of land and wealth.
Familial inheritance broadens the transfer motif, but lacks the focus verse's divine territorial grant.
The combatants' covenant and promised garden connect conflict and divine reward, while presenting it as an exchange rather than inheritance.
The judgment on hostile parties concerns the conflict setting but does not explain the ensuing inheritance.
Its concern that believers not be unknowingly trodden links to the focus verse's untraversed land and shows restrained control of conquest.
Creation of kinship and affinity does not bear on inherited territory.
The call to abandon the siege supplies local conflict context, but not the gift or transfer in 33:27.
The inheritors of Paradise preserve the central inheritance motif, though not its land-and-spoils context.
The fate of stronger earlier peoples shows that earthly strength cannot prevent God from changing possession and outcome.
The divinely decreed meeting of waters shows control over the earth, but not a transfer of land or wealth.
Reviving the earth illustrates divine power but does not clarify its bestowal to a people.
The fading of worldly growth relativizes earthly possession but does not explain inherited territory.
The exemplary conduct within the same siege narrative gives ethical context to the victory that yields the inheritance.
Paradise is explicitly made an inheritance, supporting the focus verse's presentation of a reward as a granted estate rather than a wage.
Resurrection demonstrates that God is able over all things, without addressing territorial inheritance.
The uselessness of wealth on the Last Day contrasts with the focus verse's temporal wealth but gives no transfer rationale.
Naming the faithful as inheritors directly supports the inheritance idiom, though its object is supplied by the following verse.
Forgiveness joined to power concerns mercy rather than land, homes, or spoils.
The divine aid against the besieging forces begins the same narrative sequence that culminates in 33:27.
Condemnation of consuming inheritance warns against a misuse of inherited wealth, rather than explaining its divine grant.
Bodily testimony and creation do not clarify the focus verse.
God's granting of fay without mounted military effort closely explains conquest gains as divinely conferred, not merely seized.
The Creator's sovereignty over heaven and earth is a broad foundation but lacks the focus verse's transfer theme.
The inability of wealth to protect its owners contrasts with the focus but does not illuminate its inheritance.
Household arrangements do not clarify the land, homes, or wealth granted in 33:27.
God's unrestricted power over harm and good is a general parallel only.
The swallowing of Qarun and his house demonstrates reversal of possession, but not inheritance by another people.
Noah's rescue is not linked to the focus verse's transfer of land and goods.
God makes the God-fearing inherit Paradise, directly reinforcing inheritance as a divinely assigned gift.
Legal family shares show another use of inheritance, but not divine transfer after victory.
The instruction on public dress does not clarify the focus verse.
Human power to apprehend offenders is distinct from God's power to grant a defeated people's property.
Stepping on ground that angers an enemy connects campaign movement to divinely recorded conflict, though not to inheritance itself.
Campaign spending and travel are rewarded, but they do not explain the transfer of land or goods.
God's governance from heaven to earth offers only a broad sovereignty parallel.
God's ultimate inheritance of the earth and its inhabitants establishes the divine ownership behind any temporary human inheritance.
This is the immediate siege crisis in the same narrative, whose reversal and outcome are stated in 33:26-27.
God's lordship over heaven, earth, and what lies between supports His authority over terrestrial possession.
The manipulation of sacred months does not clarify the focus verse.
Its use of fay as something God grants links the same divine-conferment vocabulary to a different legal setting.
It explicitly describes a dispossessed people's estate being made an inheritance for another people.
The request to leave no disbelieving inhabitant on earth implies dispossession but identifies no inheriting recipient.
Travel over the earth and God's creative power do not explain territorial inheritance.
The promised reversal from defeat to victory in a specified land parallels the change of power behind the focus verse.
Inheritance of scripture coupled with worldly abuse is a cautionary contrast, not support for the grant of land.
Household purification does not clarify the focus verse.
Human creation and proportioning do not bear on inherited land or spoils.
Possession of wealth and sons alone does not clarify their divine transfer.
The distribution of fay from the towns gives the social rule for divinely returned wealth rather than allowing it to circulate among the rich.
The shaking of the earth and mountains concerns final upheaval, not a grant of territory.
The call to the abode of peace does not clarify the focus verse.
The correction of kinship claims is unrelated to territorial inheritance.
The earth's leveling removes worldly elevations, but does not explain land being bestowed on a people.
The failure of personal wealth contrasts with the focus verse's wealth but offers no account of its transfer.
Established residents welcome and prefer emigrants in the same fay context, showing possession ordered toward shared provision rather than private capture.
The revival of dead earth demonstrates complete power, but not the inheritance of land.
The promise and taking of abundant spoils directly parallels the focus verse's divinely given wealth after conflict.
Rules for entering the Prophet's homes do not clarify the homes granted in 33:27.
The warning about social disorder on earth concerns alliances, not divinely assigned territorial inheritance.
The prepared garden has a broad reward parallel but no inheritance or conquest connection.
God's ownership of all in heaven and earth supports the premise that earthly property can be assigned by Him.
God's restraint of both sides after granting advantage shows that territorial and military outcomes remain under divine control.
Calling the earth God's and spacious presents land as His domain, available beyond local coercion.
The restoration of victory together with wealth, children, and numbers parallels a divinely enabled reversal of communal fortunes.
The fashioned and fruitful earth is a creation parallel, not an inheritance or transfer account.
God's action through believers to defeat and aid them supplies the conflict mechanism that precedes gains such as those in 33:27.
God's all-encompassing possession is a broad sovereignty parallel without the focus verse's power and inheritance combination.
God promises many gains, grants some immediately, and withholds hostile hands, closely matching the focus verse's bestowed conquest outcome.
The impossibility of escaping God on earth reinforces His decisive authority over every territorial setting.
God's ownership of heaven and earth joined to power over all things closely states the sovereign basis of 33:27.
Divine ownership and complete power frame punishment and forgiveness, supporting sovereignty but not a specific inheritance.
God's ability to gather all people is a general power claim with no land-transfer connection.
Power to fulfill a threatened outcome is relevant only as a generic assertion of divine capability.
Creation of heaven and earth for just recompense does not clarify the grant of land and wealth.
Exclusive dominion and measured creation establish comprehensive sovereignty, though no inheritance or conquest is in view.
Return to God and power over all things is too general to explain the particular grant.
The spreading of the earth has no connection to its being inherited by a people.
Exact justice and multiplied reward do not clarify the focus verse.
Creation of diverse creatures illustrates complete power but not bestowed territory or wealth.
Fasting provisions do not illuminate the focus verse.
Those who disbelieve cannot escape on earth, reinforcing divine control over the space whose possession is reassigned in 33:27.
Moses' request to be left alone does not clarify territorial inheritance.
The purposeful creation of heaven and earth is a broad cosmic premise, not a transfer of property.
Specified legal inheritance shares illuminate inheritance as an ordered transfer, while differing from the focus verse's collective divine grant.
The subjection of what is in heaven and earth presents earthly benefit as divine favor rather than autonomous human ownership.
Human creation, reproduction, and lifespan do not clarify inherited land or goods.
God's unique guardianship, life-giving, and complete power offer a general sovereignty parallel only.
Human vicegerency on earth supplies a broad stewardship background, not the transfer of a defeated people's estate.
The bequest rule concerns private succession and only distantly parallels the ordered transfer language of the focus verse.
God gives and removes dominion at will, providing a direct sovereignty basis for the reversal of possession in 33:27.
Men and women receiving prescribed shares concerns family inheritance, not a collective grant of land after conflict.
The specified shares of children and parents illustrate legal succession but not divine territorial inheritance.
Designated heirs and allies concern private legal succession rather than the focus verse's public transfer of estate.
God's favor in making the Children of Israel kings connects divine benefaction with communal political standing.
The command to enter the holy land God assigned to them directly presents territory as a divine allotment.
Destroyed earlier generations had been established and resourced in the earth, showing that settled possession is revocable by God.
God can remove one people and make successors after them, giving the general pattern of replacement behind the focus verse.
Making people successors in the earth frames earthly possession as a delegated and tested succession.
The people of Hud are made successors after Noah's people, illustrating divinely directed replacement of communities.
The Thamud are made successors after Aad and settled in the land, closely linking succession with territorial occupation.
Those who inherit the earth after prior inhabitants are warned by the fate of predecessors, making inheritance contingent and reversible.
Moses anticipates God destroying the enemy and making his people successors in the land, closely matching conquest followed by inheritance.
The oppressed people are explicitly made to inherit the blessed eastern and western lands after their oppressors' defeat.
God's promise of one of the two groups gives the immediate conflict-and-gain setting for divinely granted victory.
The believers' movement from weakness to shelter, support, and provision parallels a divinely effected reversal of communal condition.
The rule assigning a share of spoils to God and designated recipients places conquest wealth under divine distribution rather than private capture.
The permission to enjoy lawful good spoils confirms that battle gains are regulated divine provision.
God makes a later community successors in the earth after earlier ones, directly expressing replacement in terrestrial possession.
After the flood, Noah's party are made successors, showing survival and succession as a divine act.
Joseph is established in the land by divine purpose, giving an individual parallel for granted territorial standing.
God establishes Joseph in the land and grants him access within it, explicitly linking divine mercy to control of place and resources.
God promises to make the faithful dwell in the land after the wrongdoers, closely paralleling possession following dispossession.
God alone gives life and death and is the inheritor, grounding all human possession in God's final ownership.
The restoration of strength, wealth, and access after defeat parallels a divinely enabled reversal of communal fortunes.
After Pharaoh, the Children of Israel are told to dwell in the land, providing a direct post-oppressor settlement parallel.
God establishes Dhu al-Qarnayn in the earth and gives him means, linking territorial capacity to divine grant.
The prayer names God the best of inheritors, directly affirming divine ultimate possession behind human succession.
The righteous servants' inheritance of the earth is one of the Qur'an's clearest direct parallels to 33:27.
Those established in the land are described through their ensuing responsibilities, supplying an ethical frame for granted authority.
God promises believers succession in the earth and secure establishment after fear, directly paralleling a divinely conferred communal settlement.
The former ruling group is expelled from gardens, springs, treasures, and honorable stations, setting up the dispossession side of transfer.
The Children of Israel are explicitly made inheritors of the expelled people's estate.
Solomon's inheritance of David supports succession in authority, though not territorial inheritance after conquest.
God makes people successors in the earth, directly naming the recurring pattern of divinely assigned succession.
God wills to favor the oppressed, make them leaders, and make them inheritors, directly joining deliverance and inheritance.
God's promise to establish the oppressed in the land completes the territorial dimension of 28:5.
The inheritance of scripture is a non-territorial but explicitly divine assignment to chosen servants.
God makes people successors in the earth, supporting the focus verse's presentation of human possession as delegated succession.
The Children of Israel are made inheritors of scripture after receiving guidance, preserving the divine-transfer pattern in a different object.
God's gifts of scripture, judgment, prophethood, and good provision to the Children of Israel supply a related communal bestowal pattern.
The inheritance of heaven and earth ultimately belongs to God, reinforcing that all granted possession returns to its true owner.
God's expulsion of the People of the Book from their homes supplies the dispossession that makes the subsequent fay transfer possible.
